deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Vague Relocation Mandates

In the logistics and industrial sector, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential existential threat to your supply chain integrity. Landlords frequently draft these provisions to allow them to reclaim prime-access units for higher-rent tenants, forcing existing occupants into comparable spaces that are functionally inferior.

The trap lies in the ambiguity of the term comparable. A landlord may satisfy the literal square footage requirement while delivering a space with significantly reduced clear heights, fewer dock-high doors, or inadequate yard depth for trailer maneuvering. For a logistics operator, a loss of even 24 inches in clear height or a reduction in turning radius can render a facility useless for modern high-cube warehousing, effectively forcing a costly, unbudgeted relocation or a forced lease termination.

Furthermore, these clauses often fail to account for the massive capital expenditures required to re-configure specialized infrastructure. If the relocation requires new heavy-duty power, specialized fire suppression, or reinforced flooring, the tenant is often left holding the bill unless the lease explicitly dictates otherwise.

Securing Functional Equivalence

To mitigate this risk, a tenant must move beyond simple comparability language and insist on technical specification parity. A robust relocation clause must include the following protections:

  • Technical Specification Mandates: Explicitly define minimum clear heights, dock door counts, floor load capacities, and yard depth requirements within the lease exhibit.
  • Comprehensive Build-Out Coverage: The landlord must bear 100% of the costs for all tenant improvements, including specialized electrical, racking, or paving adjustments necessitated by the move.
  • Operational Downtime Indemnity: Provisions must require the landlord to reimburse the tenant for documented revenue losses, labor inefficiencies, and logistics disruptions incurred during the transition period.
  • Right of Refusal: The tenant must retain the absolute right to reject any space that fails to meet the pre-defined technical and operational criteria.
